title: Ashwagandha and Turmeric Lead India's Ayurveda Export Push — Evidence Is the Entry Price
excerpt: On Ayurveda Day 2026, India's export council says the botanicals are ready for global markets; the multi-herb formulations behind them still need the clinical trials to catch up.
body:
• On International Ayurveda Day 2026, India's export establishment says ashwagandha and turmeric (curcumin) — with boswellia, amla and ginger — are the botanicals ready for global supplement markets today.
  • The bottleneck is not demand but evidence and consistency: multi-herb formulations still lack strong clinical trials, and exporters must prove identity, purity, contaminant control and traceability market by market.
  • India's Ayush sector grew from $2.85 billion in 2014 to $43.4 billion in 2023, with exports doubling from $1.09 billion to $2.16 billion, government data shows.
  • The strategy is to move up the value chain — from raw herbs to standardised, scientifically characterised extracts — backed by cultivation and certification through the National Medicinal Plants Board and Quality Council of India.

Ayurveda does not need modern science to prove it has a history — but it needs modern evidence to compete in a modern marketplace. That was the message from Dr Debjani Roy, executive director of SHEFEXIL, the export promotion council under India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry, in an interview with Nutrition Insight for International Ayurveda Day 2026, observed under the theme "Ayurveda for a Healthier Tomorrow" and now marked in more than 150 countries.

Ready now — and not ready yet

Roy drew a line the wellness industry rarely draws about itself. The evidence is strongest for better-studied botanicals with defined applications — ashwagandha, turmeric (curcumin), boswellia and certain standardised extracts — which have clinical studies, mechanistic research and growing safety and standardisation data behind them. Ashwagandha, turmeric, boswellia, amla, ginger and standardised extracts are, in her assessment, positioned for international supplement markets now, provided they meet each destination's rules on identity, purity, contaminants, standardisation, safety and permitted claims.

The weaker ground is where much of traditional Ayurveda actually lives: multi-herb formulations, traditional combinations, dosage protocols and holistic claims. Those need better-designed clinical trials, standardised preparations and stronger documentation. "We should not rush every Ayurvedic ingredient into every market," Roy said. "Credibility is built by knowing when an ingredient is ready — and when it needs more science."

"India's opportunity is not merely to export Ayurveda. It is to export confidence in Ayurveda — confidence built on tradition, science, quality, sustainability, and traceability."

— Dr Debjani Roy, Executive Director, SHEFEXIL

The economics underneath

The commercial backdrop is large and growing. Government data cited by The Indian Awaaz puts the Ayush sector — Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha and Homoeopathy — at $43.4 billion in 2023, up from $2.85 billion in 2014, with exports rising from $1.09 billion to $2.16 billion over the same period. Domestic acceptance is deep: the NSSO's first all-India Ayush survey found awareness of 94.8% in rural areas and 96% in urban centres, with about half the population using Ayush systems in a year. Internationally, the WHO's Global Traditional Medicine Strategy 2025–2034 and the inclusion of Ayurveda in ICD-11's traditional medicine module have given the sector institutional scaffolding, and NITI Aayog's July 2026 roadmap to 2047 sets requirements for regulation, research and export quality.

The real barrier: consistency

Roy was blunt that demand is not the problem — curiosity about Indian botanicals is enormous. The barrier is consistent quality that foreign regulators and brands can audit: the same botanical identity, the same specifications, reliable contaminant controls, reproducible active markers and transparent supply chains. SHEFEXIL's push is to move exporters from raw herbs toward standardised ingredients, extracts and finished formulations. Sustainability is the other constraint: many botanicals are wild-harvested or grown by smallholders, so the National Medicinal Plants Board is promoting cultivation, conservation areas and a voluntary certification framework with the Quality Council of India. "If global demand grows, the answer cannot simply be 'harvest more,'" Roy said. "It has to be 'cultivate better, harvest responsibly, conserve strategically.'"

For diaspora consumers — among the most loyal buyers of ashwagandha and turmeric supplements in the US and Europe — the shift matters at the shelf: the products likeliest to survive regulatory scrutiny abroad are standardised extracts with declared active markers and traceable sourcing, not loose powders trading on tradition alone.
